title: When AI Works but Productivity Falls

body.text: You rolled out a successful AI automation to another team. Now explain why they’re less productive than before.

Imagine two customer support teams. One uses AI to draft replies to routine requests, freeing agents from repetitive writing. The business rolls the same tool out to another team: similar tickets, identical job titles, the same broad process — receive, investigate, respond. Yet its queue slows down, even though the AI works as intended. But what does "investigate" involve, and what must be true before someone can respond?

In the second team, exceptions demand context across systems and careful judgment. Reviewing, correcting, and restoring missing details now outweigh the time saved. Having worked in support, I know how easily those differences disappear in a process map.
The assumption that both teams had identical needs produced a solution looking for a problem.
Here’s my three-step recipe for avoiding that:

items: Discover: Interview frontline employees, hold two-way Q&A roundtables, shadow their work or let them describe a typical day. Ask open questions, listen without defending the solution, try seeing the work through their eyes.

Validate: Compare management and employee priorities. Neither is automatically right — check bottlenecks against workflow evidence, task frequency, business goals, and compliance and technical constraints.

Test: Build test cases covering routine work, exceptions, and judgment calls. Define metrics, run UAT with the team, and measure the whole workflow: time saved, verification, corrections, tool switching, errors, and mental effort.

body.text: You can’t improve someone’s workflow if you don’t understand their work.
